title: Mr. Deeds
full_review:
It might have been better if "Mr. Deeds" (Columbia) hadn't come to town.

Adam Sandler's uninventive remake of Frank Capra's classic is a slight, fish-out-of-water comedy that can't decide if it wants to be a sappy romance, an indictment of a moneyed culture or a slapstick comedy. If moviegoers are looking for an undemanding flick to cool off from the summer heat, "Mr. Deeds" might be a possibilty. Otherwise, rent the original 1936 version, "Mr. Deeds Goes To Town," for time better spent.

Sandler plays Longfellow Deeds, a small-town bumpkin living in Mandrake Falls, N.H., who owns a pizza shop and writes silly but sweet greeting card verses, hoping that Hallmark will one day pick them up.

His life changes when Chuck Cedar (Peter Gallagher), a slick corporate mogul, and his crony Anderson (Erick Avari) swoop into town to inform Deeds that he's inherited $40 billion from his distant relative, Preston Blake (Harve Presnell), an uncle Deeds never knew he had. The two executives spirit Deeds off to New York City where he stays in Blake's posh apartment and learns that he not only has inherited a chain of media outlets, a football team, a basketball team and a private helicopter, but also that he is now the city's most eligible bachelor.

Meanwhile, the city's tabloids are salivating to get the inside scoop on Deeds' rags-to-riches story. Mac McGrath (Jared Harris), the ruthless host of sleazy TV news magazine "Inside Access," assigns his producer Babe Bennett (Winona Ryder) to get the dirt on Deeds. Babe goes undercover as adorable sweetheart Pam Dawson, a school nurse and small-town girl in the big city, to woo Deeds.

Wearing a mike and hidden camera, Pam captures Deeds in all sorts of compromising situations (including a wild night out with tennis ace John McEnroe) that then turn up on TV. But while she's playing her conniving part, she sees what a genuinely nice guy Deeds is and begins to fall for him in earnest (a romance that is unconvincing, especially when Ryder's character transforms nearly instantly from jerk to sweetheart).

Director Steven Brill's remake uses a broad brush to paint the characters. They fall into one of two categories: the nasty rich out to accumulate more money, and wholesome, simple poor folk who inherently have a better moral compass. But, while Capra's original had some moral resonance in that Gary Cooper's Deeds purposely gave away his money to the poor during the Depression, Sandler's character dishes out $20,000 chunks indiscriminately or to various charities (ones that screenwriter Tim Herlihy hopes will get a laugh) as pointless grand gestures.

For a country yokel, Deeds becomes accustomed to his riches and power quickly, exercising his right to fire a foul-mouthed, bratty football player or using the company jet to fly Babe out to her supposed hometown in Iowa for the day. He also becomes chummy with the staff just as fast, winning them over in an instant after urging them to try out the special acoustics in the grand apartment. His personal valet, Emilio (John Turturro), a fast-footed Spaniard who can appear and disappear almost as if by magic, becomes a close confidante.

Sandler is surprisingly restrained, letting the actors around him perform the over-the-top antics. As usual, he looks like he rolled out of his trailer park and threw himself together seconds before filming. But mainly he coasts through the movie in a bland performance that is supposed to convey an "every guy" persona. However, every so often, Sandler's more sadistic side appears, as he beats someone into the ground, "Happy Gilmore"-style. These fisticuff scenes are out of sync with the film's more good-natured tone.

Ending on a corny, predictable note, "Mr. Deeds" disappoints.

Due to a few scenes of nasty fisticuffs, brief rear nudity and some crass expressions, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13. 2002
